tip: Here 'over' means across an open surface: 'over het plein' means across the square.
'Wachten' takes 'op' for waiting for something: 'wachten op de trein' means to wait for the train.
'Opstaan' splits in a main clause: 'ik sta ... op', with 'op' sent to the very end.
With 'sinds' Dutch keeps the present tense: 'ik woon sinds twee jaar' means I have lived for two years.
Dutch uses 'zit' for something seated or tucked in: 'de kat zit onder de stoel'.
Use 'elk' with het-words and 'elke' with de-words: 'elk weekend' but 'elke week'.
The accents in 'één' mark it as the number one and stress it: 'met één hand' means with just one hand.
'Uitnodigen' can split far apart: 'nodigen' and 'uit' wrap the whole middle, with 'uit' at the very end of the clause.
'Liever' means would rather or prefer to: 'blijven wij liever binnen' means we would rather stay inside.
'Goed' has an irregular comparative: 'beter', not 'goeder'. 'Een betere oplossing' means a better solution.
After a sharp sound like the 'k' in 'maken', the past tense adds '-te', not '-de': 'maken' becomes 'maakte'.
'Die' is the linking word (that/who) for de-words: 'een hond die Max heette' means a dog that was called Max.
A helper verb like 'moet' pushes the main verb to the end: 'moet ... opladen' means must top up.
'De gebeten hond' literally means the bitten dog, the Dutch image for the one everyone blames or who takes the fall.
'Hoe' twice builds 'the more... the more': 'hoe langer... hoe meer' means the longer... the more.
In goodbyes, 'nog' adds 'for the rest of', so 'prettige avond nog' wishes you a good remainder of the evening.
Say 'tot' plus a time to mean 'see you then': 'tot snel' is 'see you soon'.
Start with a time word and the verb comes next, before the subject: 'overmorgen vertrekken wij', not 'overmorgen wij vertrekken'.
Motion into something wraps the noun in 'tegen ... in': 'tegen de wind in' means straight into the wind.
For a route Dutch uses 'lopen' (to run or go), so 'het pad loopt langs de rivier' means the path runs along the river.
Dutch often names the posture instead of 'is': an upright object 'staat', so 'de stoel staat bij de tafel'.
For a future span, 'over' means 'in': 'over twee weken' is 'in two weeks', counting forward from now.
'Nooit' (never) follows the verb in a plain sentence: 'wij eten nooit vlees', not 'wij nooit eten vlees'.
'Morgen' means both 'morning' and 'tomorrow' – context tells you which.
When something has the action done to it, Dutch uses 'worden': 'wordt verstuurd' means 'is being sent'.
'Aanraden' is a splitting verb: the 'aan' detaches to the end, so 'raadt de dagschotel aan' means recommends the daily special.
'Geleden' (ago) comes after the time span: 'tien jaar geleden' means 'ten years ago'.
With 'sinds', Dutch stays in the present tense: 'sinds vorig jaar woon ik' means I have been living since last year.
The '-je' ending makes a small or countable version: 'snoep' is candy in general, 'snoepjes' are individual sweets.
After 'dat' the verb moves to the very end, so in 'dat alles goed zou komen' the words 'zou komen' close the clause.
